problem.summary: YOLOs depend on NMS post-processing, which blocks true end-to-end deployment and hurts inference latency, while the many components of YOLO architectures have never been comprehensively inspected, leaving noticeable computational redundancy and suboptimal efficiency-accuracy trade-offs.
statements: Reliance on NMS for post-processing hampers end-to-end deployment of YOLOs and adversely impacts inference latency.
One-to-many label assignment during training necessitates NMS at inference, slowing it down and making performance sensitive to NMS hyperparameters.
YOLO component design lacks comprehensive inspection from efficiency and accuracy perspectives, leaving considerable computational redundancy and constrained model capability.

evidence.quote: the reliance on the non-maximum suppression (NMS) for post-processing hampers the end-to-end deployment of YOLOs and adversely impacts the inference latency.
the design of various components in YOLOs lacks the comprehensive and thorough inspection, resulting in noticeable computational redundancy and limiting the model’s capability.
Specifically, YOLOs usually employ one-to-many label assignment strategy during training, whereby one ground-truth object corresponds to multiple positive samples.
this approach necessitates NMS to select the best positive prediction during inference. This slows down the inference speed and renders the performance sensitive to the hyperparameters of NMS
As a result, there still exists considerable computational redundancy within YOLOs, leading to inefficient parameter utilization and suboptimal efficiency.

background.summary: The paper builds on the YOLO lineage (YOLOv1-v9, Gold-YOLO, YOLO-MS) with backbone/neck/head designs and TAL assignment, and on the end-to-end DETR line (DETR, Deformable-DETR, DINO, RT-DETR) plus one-to-one CNN detectors, claiming DETRs still lag YOLOs in forward-pass efficiency and prior one-to-one CNN approaches add overhead or lose performance.

relatedWork.name: DETR
relatedWork.relation: prior end-to-end transformer detector with one-to-one Hungarian matching
relatedWork.quote: DETR [4] introduces the transformer architecture and adopts Hungarian loss to achieve one-to-one matching prediction, thereby eliminating hand-crafted components and post-processing.

relatedWork.name: RT-DETR
relatedWork.relation: prior real-time DETR and main end-to-end baseline
relatedWork.quote: RT-DETR [78] further designs the efficient hybrid encoder and proposes the uncertainty-minimal query selection to improve both the accuracy and latency.

relatedWork.name: YOLOv8
relatedWork.quote: YOLOv8 [21] presents C2f building block for effective feature extraction and fusion.

relatedWork.name: Gold-YOLO
relatedWork.relation: prior YOLO with GD feature-fusion mechanism, used as comparison
relatedWork.quote: Gold-YOLO [60] provides the advanced GD mechanism to boost the multi-scale feature fusion capability.

evidence.quote: when considering only the forward process of model during deployment, the efficiency of the DETRs still has room for improvements compared with YOLOs.
However, they usually introduce additional inference overhead or achieve suboptimal performance for YOLOs.

solution.summary: The paper presents consistent dual assignments for NMS-free training (an extra one-to-one head jointly trained with the one-to-many head under a consistent matching metric, keeping only the one-to-one head at inference) plus a holistic efficiency-accuracy driven model design (lightweight classification head, spatial-channel decoupled downsampling, rank-guided CIB blocks, large-kernel convolution and partial self-attention), yielding the YOLOv10 family.
solution.approach: Eliminate NMS via dual one-to-many/one-to-one label assignments with a consistent matching metric, and holistically redesign YOLO components for efficiency and accuracy.
components: consistent dual label assignments (one-to-many + one-to-one heads)
consistent matching metric shared by both heads
lightweight classification head with depthwise separable convolutions
rank-guided block design with the compact inverted block (CIB)
large-kernel depthwise convolution in deep stages

evidence.quote: we first present the consistent dual assignments for NMS-free training of YOLOs, which brings the competitive performance and low inference latency simultaneously.
we introduce the holistic efficiency-accuracy driven model design strategy for YOLOs.

During inference, we discard the one-to-many head and utilize the one-to-one head to make predictions. This enables YOLOs for the end-to-end deployment without incurring any additional inference cost.
To achieve prediction aware matching for both branches, we employ a uniform matching metric

For efficiency, we propose the lightweight classification head, spatial-channel decoupled downsampling, and rank-guided block design, to reduce the manifested computational redundancy and achieve more efficient architecture.

For accuracy, we explore the large-kernel convolution and present the effective partial self-attention module to enhance the model capability, harnessing the potential for performance improvements under low cost.

experiments.summary: YOLOv10 (N/S/M/B/L/X) is trained from scratch for 500 epochs on COCO and compared with YOLOv6/8/9, Gold-YOLO, YOLO-MS, RT-DETR and others in accuracy and T4 TensorRT FP16 end-to-end latency, with ablations for dual assignments, matching metric, and each efficiency/accuracy design element, plus training-cost, CPU/OpenVINO and 300-epoch comparisons in the appendix.

benchmarks.split: YOLOv10-S end-to-end ms, T4 TensorRT FP16
YOLOv10-X end-to-end ms, T4 TensorRT FP16

evidence.quote: our YOLOv10-S is 1.8× faster than RT-DETR-R18 under the similar AP on COCO, meanwhile enjoying 2.8× smaller number of parameters and FLOPs.
Compared with YOLOv9-C, YOLOv10-B has 46% less latency and 25% fewer parameters for the same performance.
our NMS-free training with consistent dual assignments significantly reduces the end-to-end latency of YOLOv10-S by 4.63ms, while maintaining competitive performance of 44.3% AP.
our YOLOv10 achieves 1.2% / 1.4% / 0.5% / 0.3% / 0.5% AP improvements, with 28% / 36% / 41% / 44% / 57% fewer parameters
YOLOv10-N / S outperforms YOLOv6-3.0-N / S by 1.5 AP and 2.0 AP, with 51% / 61% fewer parameters and 41% / 52% less computations, respectively.
the adoption of large-kernel convolution and PSA module leads to the considerable performance improvements of 0.4% AP and 1.4% AP for YOLOv10-S under minimal latency increase of 0.03ms and 0.15ms,

limitations.summary: The authors admit they could not study large-scale pre-training (e.g. Objects365) due to limited compute, and that NMS-free training still underperforms one-to-many training with NMS on small models, with the gap attributed to limited model capacity.
items: No pre-training on large-scale datasets such as Objects365 due to limited computational resources.
Performance gap between NMS-free and one-to-many+NMS training remains for small models (1.0 AP on YOLOv10-N, 0.5 AP on YOLOv10-S).
Large-kernel convolution brings no improvement for the medium scale (YOLOv10-M) due to its inherently extensive receptive field.

evidence.quote: Due to the limited computational resources, we do not investigate the pretraining of YOLOv10 on large-scale datasets, e.g., Objects365 [52].
there still exists a performance gap compared with the original one-to-many training using NMS, especially noticeable in small models.
For example, in YOLOv10-N and YOLOv10-S, the performance of one-to-many training with NMS outperforms that of NMS-free training by 1.0% AP and 0.5% AP, respectively.
it brings no improvements for large models, i.e., YOLOv10-M, due to its inherent extensive receptive field.

futureDirections.direction: Reduce the remaining NMS-free vs one-to-many+NMS performance gap to reach higher end-to-end performance.
futureDirections.quote: Based on this insight, we will explore approaches to further reduce the gap and achieve higher end-to-end performance in the future work.

equations.name: consistent matching metric
equations.expr: m(α, β) = s · p^α · IoU(b̂, b)^β

equations.name: supervision gap (1-Wasserstein)
equations.expr: A = t_o2o,i − I(i ∈ Ω)·t_o2m,i + Σ_{k∈Ω\{i}} t_o2m,k

equations.name: consistent metric relation
equations.expr: α_o2o = r · α_o2m, β_o2o = r · β_o2m (r = 1 by default)

applications.detail: Autonomous driving, robot navigation, object tracking
applications.quote: It is widely adopted in various practical applications, including autonomous driving [3], robot navigation [12], and object tracking [72], etc.

applications.detail: Authors highlight YOLO applicability to medical image analysis and autonomous driving
applications.quote: The YOLOs can be widely applied in various real-world applications, including medical image analyses and autonomous driving, etc.

deploymentClaims: Latencies of all models tested on T4 GPU with TensorRT FP16, following RT-DETR's benchmark
End-to-end latency measured on COCO val, batch size 1, with TensorRT efficientNMSPlugin post-processing
CPU inference benchmark on Intel Xeon Skylake using OpenVINO

evidence.quote: the latencies of all models are tested on T4 GPU with TensorRT FP16, following [78].
The TensorRT efficientNMSPlugin is appended for post-processing and the I/O overhead is omitted.
We present the speed comparison results of YOLOv10 and others on CPU (Intel Xeon Skylake, IBRS) using OpenVINO in Fig. 5.
We observe that YOLOv10 also shows state-of-the-art trade-offs in terms of performance and efficiency.
